summary:
We developed Project Perseverance: Survive on Mars, a browser-based survival and strategy game for kids ages 7 to 12. Inspired by NASA's Mars 2020 mission in Jezero Crater, the game puts players in charge of keeping a four-person Martian outpost alive across turns called Sols.

Most space content for kids is either too simple or way too technical, so we translated real NASA open data into hands-on engineering trade-offs. Instead of invented numbers, we used real solar storm events from NASA DONKI, radiation readings from Curiosity's RAD instrument, biological studies from NASA OSDR, and real rover photos of Jezero Crater. Players balance limited power, water, food, and radiation exposure, such as diverting greenhouse water to run a radiation shield during a solar storm or ending a spacewalk before an astronaut gets irradiated.

This project matters because it lets young students experience why mission planners have to make tough calls where no choice is free. Since it runs right in any browser with no downloads or accounts needed, teachers and families can easily use it to make real space science engaging.
details:
Project Perseverance: Survive on Mars

Project Perseverance: Survive on Mars is a browser-based survival game we built for kids ages 7 to 12. It is inspired by NASA's Mars 2020 mission in Jezero Crater, and the main idea behind it is simple: we wanted kids to experience the real engineering trade-offs astronauts face on Mars, where nothing is free and every choice affects what happens the next day. Just to be clear, it is an independent educational project using open data, not an official NASA product.

What it does and how it works

In the game, you manage a small Martian outpost across turns called Sols, which are Martian days lasting 24 hours and 39 minutes. Instead of just reading facts off a screen, players have to keep a crew of four alive by balancing power, water, food, and radiation exposure.

Each Sol plays out in a few clear steps:

* Assigning your crew and power: You start each day with limited energy cells and four specialists, and you assign them to different rooms simply by tapping an icon and then tapping a room. One of the crew members, the captain, fractured a leg during landing, and because bones heal much slower in Mars's 0.38g gravity, the captain cannot go outside on spacewalks (EVAs). That forces you to rotate the other three crew members and figure out where the captain's leadership helps most indoors.

* Surviving solar storms: Players check the space weather forecast (Clear Day, Solar Alert, or Superstorm). When a Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) approaches faster than 1,200 km/s, normal shielding is not enough, so you have to activate the Water Shield to block the radiation, which means cutting off water to your greenhouse for that Sol.

* Risk-vs-reward EVA minigames: Sending an astronaut outside in a spacesuit triggers a quick touch minigame. The catch is that every extra second outside raises radiation exposure, so you have to decide when to abort and get back to the airlock before your astronaut gets irradiated.

* Communication delays with Earth: Based on the real 178 million km distance between Earth and Mars during the January 16, 2025 opposition, radio messages take 10 minutes to travel. In the game, that means any reply from Houston does not arrive until the next Sol, and strong solar flares (X or M5+) can knock out your radio completely.

Benefits and intended impact

Most space content for elementary school kids is either too simple, like static posters, or way too technical. We wanted to hit that middle ground so students can actually feel why NASA mission planners have to make tough calls under uncertainty. While playing, kids naturally pick up real aerospace terms like ECLSS, EVA, CME, and light-time through an integrated glossary called Space Words, without feeling like they are studying for a test.

Because it runs straight in the browser with zero downloads or accounts, teachers can open it on school Chromebooks and parents can pull it up on a tablet at home. We also added multiple endings, including funny unlockable ones like opening a Martian taqueria or finding a Martian pet, so kids actually want to replay it and test new survival strategies. Plus, teachers, parents, or judges can open the sources menu at any time to inspect the exact NASA studies behind every rule.

Tools, languages, and data we used

On the software side, we built the frontend with TypeScript, React, and Tailwind CSS, locking the layout to a single viewport (100dvh) so there is no awkward scrolling on tablets or phones. We used Vite with vite-plugin-pwa so the game works offline and can be installed like a native app, Zustand with localStorage to auto-save progress after every Sol, and Vercel for hosting. We also used Claude Code to help scaffold the architecture and verify builds, pairing custom comic-style illustrations with real surface photos from the Perseverance rover (PIA24264, PIA24921, PIA25212, and PIA26373).

For the science, we grounded the game mechanics in real open datasets instead of making up numbers:

* NASA DONKI: We used 34 real historical solar flare (FLR) and CME events from 2011 to 2012 to drive the weather system and radio blackouts.

* MSL-RAD / RadLab (Curiosity): Three real surface radiation readings from Mars calibrate our damage scale: 0.982 uGy/h on a quiet day (July 3, 2023), 27.31 uGy/h during a solar alert, and 303.988 uGy/h during an extreme storm (May 20, 2024).

* NASA OSDR: Five peer-reviewed biological studies shape the crew and greenhouse rules: OSD-418 and OSD-396 for slow muscle and bone fracture recovery in 0.38g, OSD-268 (Veggie VEG-01B) for growing lettuce in space, OSD-360 for cumulative low-dose radiation damage, and OSD-566 for weakened immune responses.

* Canadian Space Agency (CSA): We pulled ideas for our greenhouse mechanics from their educational food production kit for long space missions.

What makes our project creative

What makes our approach different is that the minigames are not about button-mashing; winning means knowing when to stop before you hurt your crew. Turning a real bone-healing paper (OSD-396) into an asymmetric mechanic where your captain is restricted to indoor command also creates a fresh tactical puzzle every turn. Balancing hard dosimetry data with kid-friendly humor keeps younger players hooked while still giving older siblings or adults plenty to think about.

Factors our team considered

While designing the game, we focused heavily on not overwhelming 7-to-12-year-olds. Real radiation units like micrograys per hour (uGy/h) are hard to track mid-game, so we kept the real readings under the hood and showed kids a simple 0-100 dose bar alongside easy percentages for water, food, and power.

We also wanted to be completely honest about our data. We built a dedicated "What We Simplified (To Be Honest)" section inside the game to explain what we adapted for gameplay, such as noting that RadLab's API was down during development, so we stored those real readings with their exact dates and timestamps instead of pretending they were live. Finally, we replaced complicated drag-and-drop controls with a simple two-tap system (tap an icon, then tap a room) and large buttons so younger kids would not get frustrated on touchscreens.
